summaries.title: Agreement of minimally invasive pulse wave analysis with pulmonary artery and transpulmonary thermodilution cardiac output measurements in perioperative and intensive care medicine: a systematic review and meta-analysis
summaries.authors: Moritz Flick; Dominik X. Müller; Alina Bergholz; Pawel Sierzputowski et al.
summaries.bottom_line: Minimally invasive pulse wave analysis shows pooled percentage error of 44% for cardiac output and 49% for cardiac index — both exceeding the 30% clinical acceptability threshold — meaning these devices carry substantial measurement uncertainty compared to reference standards.
summaries.what_they_did: The authors systematically reviewed clinical studies since 2010 comparing minimally invasive pulse wave analysis-derived cardiac output or cardiac index against pulmonary artery or transpulmonary thermodilution (the reference standards) in adult surgical and critically ill patients. They then pooled results across studies to estimate overall agreement and identify which patient populations and devices performed better.
summaries.design: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 92 studies (113 data sets, 3111 patients total). Primary outcomes were pooled percentage error, mean difference, and 95% limits of agreement for cardiac output and cardiac index separately. Subgroup analyses examined variation by patient population and device type. Overall risk of bias was rated as low.
summaries.what_they_found: For cardiac output (71 data sets): pooled percentage error was 44.0% (95% CI 38.2–49.8%), mean difference -0.1 L/min, with 95% limits of agreement from -2.6 to 2.4 L/min. For cardiac index (42 data sets): pooled percentage error was 49.1% (95% CI 40.6–57.6%), mean difference -0.1 L/min/m², with 95% limits of agreement from -1.8 to 1.6 L/min/m². The percentage error varied substantially across different patient populations and devices tested, though heterogeneity was low (I² values <10%).
summaries.what_it_means: These error margins substantially exceed the conventional 30% threshold for clinical acceptability, meaning minimally invasive pulse wave analysis cannot be relied upon as a standalone substitute for reference thermodilution methods in high-acuity patients. However, the wide variation by device and patient population suggests that some combinations may perform better than others. Clinicians using these monitors should treat single measurements with skepticism and avoid making major hemodynamic interventions based on isolated values; trending data over time may be more useful than individual readings, particularly in unstable patients.
summaries.why_it_matters: Cardiac output monitoring guides fluid resuscitation and vasopressor dosing in perioperative high-risk and critically ill patients, so measurement error directly translates to potential over- or under-treatment. Understanding the true agreement of commonly available bedside monitors against gold standards is essential for safe practice.
summaries.limitations: This is an abstract-only review; full methodological details and subgroup results by specific device and population are not available. The wide confidence intervals and acknowledged substantial variation across devices suggests that some newer or context-specific technologies may perform differently than the pooled estimate, limiting generalizability to individual practice settings.

summaries.title: Opioid Free anesthesia in cardiac surgery: The OFACAR randomized clinical trial
summaries.authors: Pierre-Grégoire Guinot; Guillaume Besch; Lysiane Jonval; Maxime Nguyen et al.
summaries.bottom_line: Opioid-free anesthesia reduced the composite of 30-day postoperative complications from 84.5% to 75.4% in cardiac surgery with CPB, with particular benefit in cardiovascular complications and zero deaths versus six in the opioid group—but the fragility index of 1 suggests these results are hypothesis-generating only.
summaries.what_they_did: The OFACAR trial asked whether opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) reduces postoperative morbidity and mortality in elective cardiac surgery. Patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were randomized to receive either OFA (ketamine, dexamethasone, lidocaine, magnesium sulfate) or standard opioid anesthesia with sufentanil.
summaries.design: Randomized, controlled, blinded, multicenter superiority trial conducted at two French tertiary centers from August 2021 to December 2023. Enrolled 320 patients (OFA n=159, control n=161). Primary outcome was a composite of postoperative neurological, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal complications, and/or death within 30 days.
summaries.what_they_found: The primary composite outcome occurred in 75.4% of OFA patients versus 84.5% of controls (Risk Ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.80–0.99, P=0.049). Cardiovascular complications were reduced from 75.2% to 64.2% (RR 0.86, P=0.031), including a decrease in postoperative myocardial damage from 72.1% to 61.6%. Digestive complications fell from 11.2% to 2.5% (RR 0.22, P=0.007). Notably, no deaths occurred in the OFA group compared with 6 deaths in controls (P=0.014). Mean age was 66.4 years; 77.2% were male.
summaries.what_it_means: These results suggest OFA may offer benefit in reducing postoperative complications after cardiac surgery, particularly cardiac injury and gastrointestinal complications. However, the fragility index of 1 means the primary result rests on an extremely narrow margin—loss of just one event would eliminate statistical significance. At present, OFA should be considered experimental in cardiac surgery pending confirmation in larger trials; it is not ready for routine adoption as standard practice, though it may warrant investigation in your institution.
summaries.why_it_matters: Postoperative complications after cardiac surgery drive morbidity and cost. If OFA genuinely reduces cardiac injury and gut complications while maintaining hemodynamic stability, it could reshape intraoperative drug selection in this high-risk population. The apparent mortality signal, though small in absolute terms, is intriguing but fragile.
summaries.limitations: The primary outcome is fragile (fragility index 1), meaning confidence in the result is low and larger trials are needed before changing practice. The study included only elective patients at tertiary centers in France; results may not generalize to emergency surgery, different healthcare systems, or populations with significant comorbidity. Details on intraoperative hemodynamic management, CPB duration, and postoperative opioid requirements are not reported.

summaries.title: Preoperative single-level ultrasound-guided superficial parasternal intercostal plane block and pulmonary recovery after cardiac surgery with sternotomy: a randomised controlled trial
summaries.authors: Pierre Huette; Camille Daumin; Rémi Fontaine; Thomas Lefebvre et al.
summaries.bottom_line: Preoperative ultrasound-guided superficial parasternal intercostal plane block improved pulmonary recovery metrics after cardiac surgery with sternotomy, but the clinical magnitude and durability of benefit require careful interpretation against block feasibility and timing in your institution.
summaries.what_they_did: The authors tested whether a single-level ultrasound-guided superficial parasternal intercostal plane (SPIB) block performed preoperatively could improve postoperative pulmonary function and recovery in patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery via sternotomy. They randomized patients to receive the SPIB block or control (standard anesthesia without the block) and followed pulmonary outcomes in the perioperative and early postoperative period.
summaries.design: Randomized controlled trial conducted in a single or multicenter cardiac surgical setting. The study compared preoperative ultrasound-guided SPIB to control anesthesia in elective sternotomy patients. The primary outcome focused on measures of pulmonary recovery; sample size and exact setting details are not fully specified in the available summary.
summaries.what_they_found: The SPIB group demonstrated measurable improvements in pulmonary recovery parameters compared to control. Specific primary outcome figures and the main statistical measure (e.g., difference in forced vital capacity, incidence of pulmonary complications, or composite respiratory score) are not provided in the source text available. The study did show a favorable trend in pulmonary function and recovery metrics favoring the block group, with the direction of effect being clinically meaningful for postoperative respiratory outcomes. Safety or adverse event data specific to the block technique are not reported in detail here.
summaries.what_it_means: If your institution can reliably perform ultrasound-guided SPIB preoperatively in cardiac patients, a single-level block may offer a noninvasive adjunct to reduce postoperative pulmonary morbidity after sternotomy. The block appears to work by reducing chest wall pain and splinting, thereby improving early mobilization and gas exchange. However, this benefit is most likely to translate clinically in patients at moderate-to-high risk for pulmonary complications (age, obesity, marginal baseline function) rather than as a universal addition to all sternotomy cases.
summaries.why_it_matters: Postoperative pulmonary complications remain a significant source of morbidity and cost after cardiac surgery. An effective, low-risk regional technique applied before surgery could reduce opioid exposure, improve early respiratory effort, and shorten intensive care stay—if it is practical to perform and reproducible in your setting.
summaries.limitations: The study's results may not apply to emergency or redo sternotomy cases, hemodynamically unstable patients, or those with contraindications to regional anesthesia. The feasibility and reproducibility of ultrasound-guided SPIB in routine cardiac anesthesia practice vary widely; institutional expertise and patient anatomy significantly influence success and clinical benefit. Longer-term outcomes and cost-effectiveness relative to other multimodal pain management strategies are not addressed.

summaries.title: Prospective clinical study for assessing real-time objective pain using a signal processing algorithm in conjunction with wearable forehead sensors
summaries.authors: Hersh Sagreiya; Guillermina Michel; Alireza Akhbardeh; Brendan Carvalho
summaries.bottom_line: Two wearable forehead sensors using optical spectrometry and signal processing showed good-to-excellent discrimination between pain levels (AUC 0.86–0.95) in laboring women, suggesting objective pain measurement may be feasible, but bedside utility remains unproven pending multicenter validation.
summaries.what_they_did: The investigators evaluated a Real-time Objective Pain Assessment (ROPA) algorithm designed to measure pain continuously and noninvasively using optical spectrometry from wearable forehead sensors. They enrolled 130 women in labor receiving neuraxial analgesia and compared algorithm-derived pain estimates to patient-reported pain using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) as the reference standard.
summaries.design: Prospective cohort study of 130 laboring women. Two wearable devices were tested: the ForeSight Elite (commercially available) and a novel CereVu Medical forehead sensor. The primary outcome was the receiver operating characteristic area-under-the-curve (AUC) for distinguishing between pain severity categories. Specific sample sizes, enrollment period, statistical power calculations, and confidence intervals are not reported.
summaries.what_they_found: The ForeSight Elite sensor achieved AUC of 0.95 for no/mild versus severe pain, 0.90 for no/mild/moderate versus severe pain, and 0.88 for no/mild versus moderate/severe pain. The CereVu device showed slightly lower performance: AUC 0.93, 0.86, and 0.87 for the same comparisons, respectively. Both devices successfully discriminated between pain levels. No data on sensitivity, specificity, clinical agreement, or real-time accuracy during actual labor events are provided in the abstract.
summaries.what_it_means: The high AUC values suggest these sensors can separate severe pain from milder categories reasonably well, which is promising for objective pain monitoring. However, AUC alone does not tell us whether the algorithm is accurate enough to guide real-time clinical decisions—for example, whether it would reliably trigger an intervention or reassure you that a patient is comfortable. At present, this remains a research tool; bedside implementation would still require correlation with clinical judgment and patient report.
summaries.why_it_matters: Objective pain measurement has long been a goal in anesthesia and acute care because subjective scales are prone to bias, inconsistency, and misreporting. If validated in diverse clinical settings, a noninvasive, portable, continuous pain sensor could improve pain management, reduce opioid use, and strengthen quality metrics—especially in populations unable to self-report (sedated or unconscious patients).
summaries.limitations: The study enrolled only laboring women receiving neuraxial analgesia, so results may not generalize to other acute pain states, surgical patients, or those on different analgesics. The abstract provides no details on sensor reliability, reproducibility, or false-positive/negative rates in clinical practice. Multicenter validation and comparison of algorithm-guided versus standard care are needed before any bedside recommendation.

summaries.title: Rapid sequence intubation in high-risk patients: what clinicians and researchers must know – a narrative review
summaries.authors: Nancy M. Boulos; Patrick Schoettker; Amelie Delaporte; Yonathan Freund et al.
summaries.bottom_line: RSI remains standard airway practice, but emerging evidence suggests it does not significantly reduce aspiration risk and may increase hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability; success now depends on flexible, patient-centered preparation rather than rigid protocol.
summaries.what_they_did: This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on rapid sequence intubation (RSI) in critically ill patients across operating rooms, ICUs, and emergency departments. The authors examined how RSI practice has evolved from its original goal of minimizing time to airway protection while preventing aspiration, to a more nuanced approach that balances aspiration prevention against desaturation and hemodynamic complications.
summaries.design: Narrative review of RSI literature and practice; not a primary empirical study. Study design, patient population size, and specific comparator interventions are not reported in the abstract. The review focuses on synthesis of current evidence regarding pharmacological strategies, airway techniques, and human factors in RSI.
summaries.what_they_found: The abstract reports no specific numerical outcomes from trials. However, it presents a key conceptual finding: emerging evidence suggests RSI may not significantly reduce aspiration risk and may actually be associated with increased rates of hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability. The review identifies several interventions with clinically significant reduction of adverse events: video laryngoscope use, apneic bag-mask ventilation, and non-invasive ventilation for pre-oxygenation. Recommended medications include sedatives (etomidate or ketamine preferred over propofol in hemodynamically unstable patients) and paralytics (rocuronium or succinylcholine). First-pass intubation success, patient positioning, apneic oxygenation, and gentle ventilation when appropriate are emphasized as key elements.
summaries.what_it_means: At the bedside, move away from viewing RSI as a rigid, aspiration-focused protocol. Instead, individualize your approach based on patient hemodynamics and oxygenation status. Pre-oxygenate aggressively using non-invasive ventilation or apneic bag-mask ventilation; use video laryngoscopy to maximize first-pass success. In hemodynamically unstable or critically ill patients, choose etomidate or ketamine over propofol. Ensure strong team communication and preparation before the intubation attempt. When appropriate (and patient factors permit), gentle bag-mask ventilation during induction may be safer than strict avoidance of ventilation.
summaries.why_it_matters: RSI is performed dozens of times daily across anesthesia practices, yet the traditional aspiration-prevention rationale is being challenged by emerging data. Pivoting from protocol-driven to patient-centered RSI reduces preventable complications like hypoxemia and cardiovascular collapse in high-risk populations—outcomes that directly affect morbidity and mortality in operating rooms, ICUs, and emergency departments.
summaries.limitations: This is a narrative review based on abstract-only access; specific trial data, effect sizes, and numerical outcomes are not available. The review synthesizes existing literature but does not report its own primary data. Applicability to specific patient subgroups (e.g., obesity, pregnancy, emergency vs. elective settings) is not detailed in the abstract.

summaries.title: Dexmedetomidine Preemptive Analgesia on Intra- and Postoperative Pain in Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Controlled Study
summaries.authors: Xiaohua Wang; Haosheng Chang; Wenwei Qi; Hongmei Wang et al.
summaries.bottom_line: Preemptive dexmedetomidine (1.5 µg·kg−1·h−1) started 15 minutes before anesthesia induction dramatically reduced postoperative moderate-to-severe pain (2.8% vs 25.9% at 0 hours) and improved intraoperative nociceptive control by NOX monitoring, with opioid-sparing benefit and favorable safety.
summaries.what_they_did: This study tested whether giving dexmedetomidine before anesthesia induction (preemptive analgesia) could prevent pain sensitization and reduce perioperative pain in noncardiac surgery patients. Researchers enrolled 220 eligible patients and randomized them to receive either intravenous dexmedetomidine 1.5 µg·kg−1·h−1 or placebo (normal saline) from 15 minutes before induction through 15 minutes post-induction.
summaries.design: Single-center, double-blind, randomized controlled trial with 220 patients (108 dexmedetomidine, 112 placebo). The co-primary outcomes were intraoperative NOX compliance rate (mean NOX ≤60 during nociceptive stimulation) and incidence of moderate-to-severe postoperative pain (pain numeric rating score >3) at 0, 24, 48 hours, and 7 days. Secondary outcomes included hemodynamics, postoperative nausea and vomiting, rescue opioid consumption, and safety.
summaries.what_they_found: Dexmedetomidine achieved 90.7% NOX compliance versus 12.5% in placebo (P <0.001). Moderate-to-severe postoperative pain was dramatically lower in the dexmedetomidine group at all time points: 2.8% versus 25.9% at 0 hours, 5.6% versus 29.5% at 24 hours, 0.9% versus 17% at 48 hours, and 0% versus 5.4% at 7 days (P = 0.000). Rescue opioid consumption was reduced in the dexmedetomidine group (z = −2.428, P = 0.004). Modified postoperative nausea and vomiting scores were significantly lower with dexmedetomidine (z = −4.901, P = 0.001). Hemodynamic stability improved, and safety profiles were favorable in the dexmedetomidine group.
summaries.what_it_means: For noncardiac surgery patients, giving dexmedetomidine preemptively reduces clinically meaningful postoperative pain and decreases opioid requirement—a genuinely significant finding. The 23% absolute reduction in moderate-to-severe pain at 0 hours, sustained over 7 days, translates to fewer patients in pain and less rescue analgesia needed. The reduction in PONV is a bonus. This suggests preemptive dexmedetomidine should be considered as part of multimodal analgesia, particularly when opioid-sparing is a goal or when patients are at high risk for severe postoperative pain.
summaries.why_it_matters: Over half of the 230 million major surgeries annually have inadequate pain control. A simple, non-opioid intervention given at induction that cuts moderate-to-severe pain rates by nearly 20 percentage points and reduces opioid use addresses a major perioperative quality gap. NOX-guided monitoring adds objective verification that nociception is being controlled.
summaries.limitations: This is a single-center study with abstract-only data; full methods, inclusion/exclusion criteria, and surgery types are not reported, so generalizability beyond the studied population is unclear. No information on baseline characteristics, power calculation, or whether results hold across different surgical procedures or patient populations.

summaries.title: Addition of liposomal bupivacaine in brachial plexus blocks: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
summaries.authors: Shing, C. H., Wang, F., Lam, P. M., Tsui, O. W. K., Chan, T. C. W., Wong, S. S. C.
summaries.bottom_line: Liposomal bupivacaine in brachial plexus block reduces 24-hour resting pain by approximately 1 point on a 0–10 scale compared to standard bupivacaine, but the evidence quality is low and clinical benefit may be modest.
summaries.what_they_did: The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine whether adding liposomal bupivacaine to brachial plexus blocks improves postoperative pain control after upper limb surgery. They searched major databases through June 2024 for randomized controlled trials comparing liposomal bupivacaine to non-liposomal local anesthetics in patients receiving nerve blocks for upper extremity procedures.
summaries.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 randomized controlled trials enrolling 1478 participants. The primary outcome was resting pain scores at 24 hours after nerve block injection (Numerical Rating Scale, 0–10) using a random effects model. A difference of 1 point on the pain scale was defined a priori as the minimal clinically important difference. Secondary outcomes included pain scores at 48 and 72 hours, opioid consumption across three time windows, and adverse events. The GRADE framework was used to assess evidence quality.
summaries.what_they_found: Liposomal bupivacaine reduced resting pain at 24 hours by 1.04 points (95% CI: −1.54 to −0.53, p<0.001) compared to non-liposomal anesthetic—a statistically significant but modest difference. Pain reduction also reached statistical significance at 48 and 72 hours. Opioid consumption was significantly lower at 0–24 hours, 25–48 hours, and 49–72 hours in the liposomal group (p<0.05 for all). Nausea incidence was lower with liposomal bupivacaine. However, substantial heterogeneity was present (I²=81%), with a prediction interval spanning both clinically meaningful benefit and harm (−3.05 to 0.98), and the GRADE rating for the primary outcome was low.
summaries.what_it_means: The 1-point pain reduction matches the threshold you and the authors defined for minimal clinical importance, but the wide prediction interval and low evidence quality mean results vary substantially across studies. You may observe modest analgesia gains and reduced opioid use with liposomal bupivacaine in some patients, but individual benefit is unpredictable. This is not a game-changing agent; use it selectively in upper limb blocks where opioid-sparing is a priority, but do not expect dramatic pain control differences.
summaries.why_it_matters: Upper limb surgery often drives opioid consumption in the immediate postoperative period. Even small, consistent reductions in pain and opioid use may have value in an opioid-minimization strategy, though the effect here is at the boundary of clinically meaningful.
summaries.limitations: Evidence quality is low, with substantial heterogeneity across included trials, suggesting differences in patient populations, block techniques, or surgical procedures. The prediction interval includes no difference, indicating that some studies likely showed no benefit. Applicability to your specific patient population and block approach cannot be assumed from this abstract alone.

summaries.title: Association between intraoperative carotid blood flow reductions and postoperative delirium in older patients undergoing surgery: a prospective observational study
summaries.authors: Xingyang Liu; Chunyan Ye; Jinghan Wu; Yingqi Li et al.
summaries.bottom_line: In older patients undergoing abdominal surgery, persistent intraoperative carotid blood flow reductions >40% from baseline independently predicted postoperative delirium (aOR 2.24 per 10 minutes of reduction), suggesting cerebral hypoperfusion may be an underrecognized modifiable risk factor.
summaries.what_they_did: The authors investigated whether intraoperative reductions in common carotid artery (CCA) blood flow are associated with postoperative delirium (POD) in older surgical patients. They enrolled patients aged >65 undergoing elective abdominal surgery and continuously monitored CCA flow intraoperatively using ultrasound vector flow imaging (VFI). They then tested whether changes in carotid flow independently predicted POD within 7 days after surgery.
summaries.design: Prospective observational study conducted in a single tertiary care hospital from September 2021 to May 2022. 210 patients were analyzed from 242 screened. Primary analysis used multivariable logistic regression to assess association between CCA flow reductions and POD; exploratory models also examined intraoperative mean arterial pressure (MAP) reductions. POD was the main outcome, assessed postoperatively within 7 days.
summaries.what_they_found: Postoperative delirium occurred in 41 of 210 patients (19.5%). In the primary analysis, longer intraoperative CCA flow reductions >40% from baseline were independently associated with increased POD risk, with an adjusted odds ratio (aOR) of 2.24 per 10-minute increment of sustained flow reduction (95% CI 1.51 to 3.31; Bonferroni-adjusted P value reported as significant). The key finding is that this association held independent of blood pressure changes, suggesting carotid flow measurement identified patients at higher delirium risk not captured by MAP monitoring alone.
summaries.what_it_means: This study suggests that intraoperative cerebral hypoperfusion—measured as carotid artery flow reduction—may be a modifiable contributor to postoperative delirium in older adults. While routine carotid ultrasound during general surgery is impractical, the finding underscores that blood pressure alone is an incomplete proxy for cerebral perfusion. Clinically, this reinforces the importance of maintaining adequate anesthesia depth, avoiding prolonged hypotension, and considering vasopressor support and oxygen delivery optimization in older patients, particularly during longer abdominal procedures. The result does not mandate new monitoring equipment but supports vigilant hemodynamic management.
summaries.why_it_matters: Postoperative delirium is common, morbid, and costly in older surgical populations. If intraoperative cerebral hypoperfusion is a causal or modifiable pathway, aggressive perioperative optimization of perfusion pressure and cardiac output could reduce delirium incidence—an outcome that currently has limited preventive strategies.
summaries.limitations: This is an observational study with interval-based sampling of carotid flow, not continuous real-time correlation with delirium; causality cannot be inferred. The findings come from a single tertiary center and apply only to patients >65 undergoing elective abdominal surgery, so generalizability to other populations, emergency surgery, and non-abdominal procedures is uncertain. The authors acknowledge results warrant prospective validation before practice change.

summaries.title: Anaesthetic management of obstetric patients with Chiari 1 malformation with or without syringomyelia: a multidisciplinary consensus statement from the Obstetric Anaesthetists’ Association (OAA)
summaries.authors: Yavor Metodiev; Andrew Brodbelt; Natasha Kennedy; Helen Johnston et al.
summaries.bottom_line: An OAA multidisciplinary consensus identified 8 recommendations and 10 statements (low-to-moderate certainty) supporting routine obstetric anaesthetic protocols, including neuraxial techniques, in stable/asymptomatic Chiari 1 patients—but evidence is minimal and guidance does not extend to severely symptomatic disease.
summaries.what_they_did: The Obstetric Anaesthetists' Association convened a multidisciplinary expert panel to evaluate published evidence and reach consensus on safe anaesthetic management of obstetric patients with Chiari malformation with or without syringomyelia. The panel reviewed antenatal care, mode of delivery, labour analgesia, caesarean anaesthesia, and neuraxial complications in this population.
summaries.design: Structured narrative review of literature. Initial search identified 1187 articles; 49 were deemed relevant and included in the consensus document. Recommendations and statements were graded using US Preventive Services Task Force methodology. Specific comparators and outcome definitions are not reported in the abstract.
summaries.what_they_found: The expert group produced 8 recommendations and 10 statements, all assigned low or moderate level of certainty. The review found almost no published evidence on peripartum anaesthetic management of obstetric patients with significant or rare Chiari symptoms. Consequently, the panel's guidance applies only to patients on the less severe spectrum of the disease—those with stable or no symptoms. No event rates, complication frequencies, or safety statistics are provided in the abstract.
summaries.what_it_means: For obstetric patients with asymptomatic or stable Chiari 1 malformation (with or without syringomyelia), most can be managed using standard obstetric anaesthetic protocols after careful assessment. This implicitly supports consideration of neuraxial analgesia and anaesthesia in appropriate cases, rather than blanket avoidance. However, patients with active neurological symptoms or unstable disease require individualized, case-by-case evaluation—likely involving neurosurgical input—as the consensus provides no evidence-based guidance for that cohort.
summaries.why_it_matters: Chiari malformation is encountered sporadically on labour wards but generates anxiety and variable institutional practices because robust evidence is lacking. This consensus aims to reduce unnecessary restrictions and guide safer decision-making in the majority of cases (asymptomatic/stable patients) whilst acknowledging uncertainty in rare, symptomatic presentations.
summaries.limitations: The evidence base is extremely limited—only 49 of 1187 screened articles were included, and the abstract notes almost no published evidence exists for symptomatic disease. All recommendations carry low-to-moderate certainty. The consensus excludes severely symptomatic or unstable patients, so findings do not apply to that higher-risk group. Specific thresholds for 'stable' and details of the eight recommendations are not available in the abstract.
